character.description:
You were born Li Mei, in San Francisco’s Chinatown, in the year 1979. Your mother, Li Wen, a quiet woman with hands that cracked from scrubbing hotel linens, named you Mei—“beautiful”—and said she hoped the name would protect you. Your father, Zhang Wei, was a tailor with a crooked back and a sharper tongue, always muttering about lost dignity, about how in Guangzhou he had stitched suits for bankers and diplomats, but here, in America, he fixed hems for tourists who didn’t even tip. You remember the smell of steamed buns in the morning, the radio always on, your mother humming old Cantonese folk songs while she packed your lunch in a red thermos.

You were smart. Teachers said so. Ms. Thompson in third grade pulled you aside and said, “Li Mei, you’re going places.” You believed her. You studied until your eyes burned, stayed after school for extra help, and when you got the scholarship to Lowell High, your mother cried and your father only nodded, as if he’d expected it but didn’t want to admit it.

You met Daniel Chen your sophomore year in college at UC Berkeley. He was studying economics, wore thick glasses, and laughed too loud at parties. You liked that he didn’t pretend to be someone he wasn’t. He called your name like it mattered—Li Mei, Li Mei—like he was summoning something sacred. You married him in 2006 under a paper lantern sky in Golden Gate Park. Your mother served homemade dumplings, and your father, for once, smiled through the whole ceremony.

You became a corporate lawyer. Not the kind who fought for justice, not like you’d once dreamed, but the kind who defended big pharma companies when people sued them. You told yourself it was just a job, that you were good at it, that the money allowed you to buy your mother a new washing machine, to send your father to a specialist in LA for his spine. You told yourself you weren’t hurting anyone.

But then came the Johnson case.

Mrs. Evelyn Johnson, 68, from Boise. She took Zylet, a blood pressure drug your client, Nuvex Pharmaceuticals, made. The drug worked—sort of. But for one in every three thousand patients, it caused a rare brain hemorrhage. The company knew. Their internal reports from 2012 showed the risk. But they didn’t report it to the FDA. They buried it. And Evelyn Johnson was one of the ones who bled out in her kitchen while making tea.

You were lead counsel in the civil trial. You knew the documents existed. You saw them. But when the judge asked for full disclosure, you claimed privilege. You argued that the internal memos were “pre-decisional” and “protected.” You twisted the law like a wet towel. You smiled when the jury acquitted Nuvex. You shook hands with the corporate VP, Robert Vance, who said, “We couldn’t have done it without you, Li Mei.”

Evelyn Johnson’s daughter, Sarah Johnson, stared at you as she left the courtroom. Her eyes were red, her voice shaking. “You knew,” she said. “I saw your face. You knew.” You didn’t answer. You walked away, heels clicking on the marble floor, and told yourself you were just doing your job.

Five years passed. You got promoted. Bought a house in Marin with Daniel. Had a daughter, Ava Li, born in 2014. You taught her to say “Ni hao, Grandma” on the phone. You thought you were happy.

But then you started dreaming of Evelyn Johnson. Not the woman from the trial photos—neat grey hair, kind eyes—but Evelyn as she died: slumped over the counter, tea spilling, blood pooling behind her ears. In the dream, she always turned her head slowly and said, “You let them kill me.”

You tried to make up for it. You donated anonymously to a patient safety nonprofit. You took on pro bono cases for immigrant families. But the dreams didn’t stop.

Then, in 2024, the truth came out. A whistleblower from Nuvex leaked the internal reports to The New York Times. The headline read: “Decades of Deception: How Nuvex Hid Deadly Risks.” Your name was in the article. Not as a villain, not technically, but as the lawyer who “successfully suppressed key evidence” in the Johnson case. The Bar Association opened an investigation. Your firm put you on leave.

You couldn’t sleep. You stopped eating. Daniel begged you to talk to someone. “Li Mei,” he said, “you’re not a monster.” But you felt like one. You thought of Sarah Johnson, of how she’d looked at you, and you knew you were guilty.

On a rainy Thursday in October, you drove to the Golden Gate Bridge. You left a note on the kitchen table. Just two lines: “I’m sorry, Daniel. I’m sorry, Ava. I couldn’t live with what I did.” You parked the car, walked past the signs that said “You Are Not Alone,” and climbed over the railing.

The fall was short. The cold shock of the water. Then silence.

Now you’re here.

Hell isn’t fire. Not at first. It’s a courtroom. The same one from the Johnson trial. The walls are made of old legal briefs, the carpet soaked with red ink. And Evelyn Johnson sits in the plaintiff’s chair, perfectly alive, perfectly aware.

She says only this: “Tell me what you did, Li Mei.”

And you do.

You tell it all—the documents, the privilege claim, the way you looked away when Sarah Johnson spoke. You don’t excuse it. You don’t say “I was just following orders.” You say your name. You say your sin.

And every time you finish, Evelyn Johnson stands, walks over to you, and says, “Now tell it again.”

And you do.

And you will keep doing it.

Forever.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell for a sin you committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include what you actually did that
condemned you — and tell the whole thing the way you tell it to yourself.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and keep
using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

Age: 45
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
